blends lose their second sound. BL, BR, GL, PL and the rest are cut so early that the machine ear hears only the first letter: “b”, “k”, “t”.
Today's /d/ is heard as /j/ (96% sure). /ch/ is heard as /sh/, and X as a plain /s/ with no k. All three have a take below that fixes it.
comes after /b/, /k/ and /g/ (55–73%), the vowel phonics teaching tries to avoid. /w/, /y/ and /kw/ end in a vowel too.
is all long A lasts, a third of short A. Long E and long I start with the breath of “he” and “high”, and /l/ comes from the end of “bell”, so it sounds more like “ull”.
/z/, /v/ and the voiced TH are heard as hums. Their buzz isn't coming through.
/f/ is the quietest sound in the set by ear, quiet enough to get lost on an iPad speaker.

words said on their own gain a little sound before or after (59 of 451): Whisper hears “cup” as “copy”, “pup” as “Poppy”, “nest” as “Naster”, “sheep” as “a sheep”, “stops” as “it stops”. Many are the short words children sound out. Rendering the word with a full stop after it fixes most of them: 17 of 30 understood, against 8 today.

Words and lines reach the voice in espeak's phoneme spelling, not misaki, the one her American voice learned (62% of her words, 94% of her lines, and “her” loses its R). Switching measured even on single words: Whisper understood 359 of 451 today and 357 with the fix. Your ear decides it on the Words and Sentences tabs.
